newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood hits Afghan Taleban as Rabbani and Dostum meet.
newsitem.headline: Masood hits Afghan Taleban as Rabbani and Dostum meet.

text.p: Afghanistan's ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani and Uzbek warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum met on Tuesday to explore forming a common front, as forces loyal to Rabbani's military chief Ahmad Shah Masood counterattacked Taleban forces.

Taleban fighters said Commander Basir Solangi, Masood's commander who withdrew north into territory controlled by Dostum as the Taleban pushed north from Kabul, attacked through the Salang Pass and over the mountainsides.
The Taleban fighters said Dostum's men were not involved in the fighting, in which the two sides exchanged artillery, mortar and small arms fire throughout the day.
The meeting between Rabbani and Dostum in Dostum's stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif was the first in three years.

General Dostum told reporters Masood was also expected in Mazar-i-Sharif by Wednesday. Dostum aides said virtually every leader of an anti-Taleban faction would be coming to Mazar-i-Sharif, including a representative of the Afghan king in exile.

The gathering in Mazar-i-Sharif leant support to a statement by Afghanistan's ambassador to India who told a news conference that Dostum had sent a message announcing support for Rabbani, whose government fled Kabul ahead of the Taleban advance.
"He (Dostum) is also in the coalition government of President Rabbani...I am informed they have come together," Ambassador Masood Khalili told reporters in New Delhi.
Press aides to Dostum said there probably would be no statements from anyone involved in the Mazar-i-Sharif meeting until Wednesday at the earliest.
Dostum controls six northern Afghan provinces and the Taleban controls about three-quarters of the country's 33 provinces.

Iranian television said on Monday night that Rabbani told its correspondent in Afghanistan that his government was regrouping to move against the Taleban, which captured the capital Kabul two weeks ago.
The Taleban offensive against the valley stronghold of Masood had stalled after meeting resistance a few hundred metres (yards) into the gorge.
There was no firm word on the outcome of Tuesday's fighting, but the Taleban fighters said their front lines, previously some five km (three miles) from Dostum's Uzbeks, had pushed forward.
The fighting, which drew Taleban forces from their attempt to thrust into the Panjsher, increased the tensions between Dostum and the Taleban.
"Dostum gave the order for the attack," said one Taleban fighter manning a road block in the Salang Pass.
Dostum moved armour and men south of the Salang Tunnel, a choke point on the road from Kabul through the Hindu Kush to his base at Mazar-i-Sharif, as the Taleban took the Afghan capital.
Word of Dostum's apparent pledge of allegiance came as the international outcry over the Taleban's treatment of women snowballed.
The Taleban on Tuesday rejected the criticisms, saying saying that while it would make changes, it would not compromise on the Islamic pillars of its policies.
"For the last 1,400 years no change has occurred in Islam. These principles are eternal and will remain eternal," acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.

But U.N. and other aid groups said after a meeting with acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammed Ghaus they were optimistic a compromise could be made that would allow them to resume operations employing and supporting women in the country.

Representative of U.N. and non-government groups, whose operations have largely ground to a halt since the Taleban takeover on September 27, said they had expressed concern and called for a return to the status quo of 11 days ago.

Thousands of educated Afghans have fled the capital saying they cannot live under strict rules that require most women to stay home, most girls to forego education and men to grow beards and attend prayers five times a day.

"We pointed out to the foreign minister there is not enough security if people do not have sufficient food. Ghaus said 'wait slowly, it will be done', but the agencies' common point was that there is not enough time and we are running out of it," Thierry Pitzner, head of the Kabul office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told reporters.

The agencies' point was reinforced by a U.N. report received by Reuters on Tuesday that said Afghan farmers, desperate to make a living, are growing more opium poppies in defiance of edicts issued by Taleban radicals.
Opium output rose to about 2,248 tonnes in 1996, a nine percent increase over 2,066 tonnes in 1995, according to a report by the U.N. International Drug Control Programme.
The report said Helmand province in the south and Nangarhar province in the east accounted for some 80 percent of all poppy cultivation in Afghanistan.
Heroin is refined from opium using chemical additives.
Helmand has been under Taleban control for more than a year.
